raw_evidence.label: The demographic 'trilemma' framing
raw_evidence.content: The Economist's 2019 framing rests on a trilemma the data is meant to dramatise: Israel is committed to being (a) Jewish-majority, (b) democratic, and (c) in control of the entire territory between the Jordan river and the Mediterranean. raw_evidence.label: The crossover year (Arabs first equal/exceed Jews): 2018
raw_evidence.content: On the data — and treating 2019-2021 as projections — the Arab total first exceeds the Jewish total in 2018, with 6,669,571 Arabs and 6,669,138 Jews: a gap of just 433 people between the river and the sea. By 2021 the gap had widened to 134,394 in the Arab column's favour. The 2018 line is so narrow that any reasonable error bar would put the actual crossover anywhere from 2017 to 2019. The point is not that one community is replacing another — both are growing — but that the territory The Economist's framing depends on (the entire Holy Land) no longer has a Jewish majority.

    print("Arab total never reaches Jewish total in this 1998-2021 window.")
else:
    first_year = int(crossed["year"].iloc[0])
    print(f"First year Arabs >= Jews: {first_year}")
    row = crossed.iloc[0]
    print(f"  Jews:  {int(row.jews_total):,}")
    print(f"  Arabs: {int(row.arabs_total):,}")
    print(f"  Gap:   {int(row.gap):,}")
# Also report 1998 vs 2021 in detail
first = totals.iloc[0]
last = totals.iloc[-1]
print(f"1998: Jews {int(first.jews_total):,} ({first.jewish_share_pct:.1f}%) vs Arabs {int(first.arabs_total):,} ({first.arab_share_pct:.1f}%)")
print(f"2021: Jews {int(last.jews_total):,} ({last.jewish_share_pct:.1f}%) vs Arabs {int(last.arabs_total):,} ({last.arab_share_pct:.1f}%)")
print(f"Jewish-share change 1998->2021: {first.jewish_share_pct - last.jewish_share_pct:+.1f} pp (decline)")

raw_evidence.label: The crossover year (Arabs first equal/exceed Jews): 2018
raw_evidence.content: On the data — and treating 2019-2021 as projections — the Arab total first exceeds the Jewish total in 2018, with 6,669,571 Arabs and 6,669,138 Jews: a gap of just 433 people between the river and the sea. By 2021 the gap had widened to 134,394 in the Arab column's favour. The 2018 line is so narrow that any reasonable error bar would put the actual crossover anywhere from 2017 to 2019. The point is not that one community is replacing another — both are growing — but that the territory The Economist's framing depends on (the entire Holy Land) no longer has a Jewish majority.

raw_evidence.label: Settler totals as published benchmarks
raw_evidence.content: External published numbers give us a sanity check on the West Bank Jewish column. Peace Now reported the West Bank settler population (excluding East Jerusalem) at around 427,800 in 2018; The Economist's CSV shows 425,599 for the same year — within roughly half a percent. By 2023 Peace Now-derived figures crossed half a million; Statista and PBS picked up the same milestone. The CSV's 2019-2021 numbers are projections from construction tenders, but they sit on the trajectory implied by every external source. So readers can take the trend as real, not as Economist-internal modelling.

raw_evidence.label: West Bank settlers grew ~2.2x as fast as Israel proper
raw_evidence.content: Between 1998 and 2021, the Jewish population of Israel proper grew 1.41x, East Jerusalem grew 1.47x, and the West Bank settler count grew 3.06x. The settler growth rate was 2.17x as fast as inside Israel itself. This isn't natural increase alone — Israel has never recorded a Jewish total fertility rate above the West Bank settler rate by anything close to 2x. The differential is driven by ongoing settlement construction, internal migration, and the heavily haredi makeup of large settlements like Modi'in Illit and Beitar Illit.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_10: Settlers grow much faster than Israel proper ---
print("=== ana_10 ===")
first = jews.iloc[0]
last = jews.iloc[-1]
print(f"Israel proper Jews 1998: {int(first['Israel']):,} -> 2021: {int(last['Israel']):,} (x{last['Israel']/first['Israel']:.2f})")
print(f"West Bank settlers 1998: {int(first['West.Bank']):,} -> 2021: {int(last['West.Bank']):,} (x{last['West.Bank']/first['West.Bank']:.2f})")
print(f"East Jerusalem Jews 1998: {int(first['East.Jerusalem']):,} -> 2021: {int(last['East.Jerusalem']):,} (x{last['East.Jerusalem']/first['East.Jerusalem']:.2f})")
mult_settler = (last['West.Bank']/first['West.Bank']) / (last['Israel']/first['Israel'])
print(f"\nWest Bank settler growth was {mult_settler:.2f}x as fast as Israel proper")

West Bank settlers 1998: 165,540 -> 2021: 506,558 (x3.06)
East Jerusalem Jews 1998: 158,155 -> 2021: 233,124 (x1.47)

West Bank settler growth was 2.17x as fast as Israel proper

raw_evidence.label: What the Green Line is and why distance from it matters
raw_evidence.content: The Green Line is the 1949 armistice line that separated Israel from Jordanian-controlled West Bank and Egyptian-controlled Gaza until the 1967 Six-Day War. Its name comes literally from the green grease pencil used on the armistice map. Since 1967 it has functioned as the de-facto reference border in every serious peace plan: settlements close to the line are inside what negotiators call 'consensus blocs' (Gush Etzion, Ma'ale Adumim, Modi'in Illit, Ariel) that Israel would expect to keep through a land swap; settlements deep beyond it are the ones any two-state agreement would require evacuating. So the 0-2.5 km, 2.5-5 km, 5-15 km, and >15 km buckets in the dataset are not just geometric — each one corresponds to a different political category. Around 75-85% of West Bank settlers live close to the Green Line in major blocs adjacent to Israeli urban areas; the residual that live deep inside the West Bank are the politically hardest to relocate.

raw_evidence.label: Settler population by distance from the Green Line, 2021
raw_evidence.content: In 2021, of the 739,682 Jews living beyond the 1967 Green Line, 31.5% were in East Jerusalem, 24.3% within 2.5 km of the line, 18.8% in the 2.5-5 km band, 15.2% between 5 and 15 km, and 10.2% deeper than 15 km. Looking at the West Bank only (506,558 settlers, excluding East Jerusalem), 62.8% live within 5 km of the Green Line — the 'consensus bloc' territory most peace plans assume Israel would keep through a land swap (det_06) — while 14.9% live deeper than 15 km, exactly the population that any two-state agreement would require evacuating.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_07: Settlers by distance from Green Line ---
print("\n=== ana_07 ===")
print(ej_wb.to_string(index=False))
# Compute the share each bucket holds in 2021
last = ej_wb.iloc[-1]
buckets = ["East.Jerusalem", "0-2.5km", "2.5-5km", "5-15km", ">15km"]
total_2021 = sum(last[b] for b in buckets)
print(f"\n2021 totals across all buckets: {int(total_2021):,}")
print("2021 share by bucket:")
for b in buckets:
    pct = 100 * last[b] / total_2021
    print(f"  {b:15} {int(last[b]):>9,} ({pct:5.1f}%)")

# Compute share within West Bank only (excluding East Jerusalem)
print("\nWithin West Bank (excluding East Jerusalem):")
wb_only = sum(last[b] for b in buckets if b != "East.Jerusalem")
for b in ["0-2.5km", "2.5-5km", "5-15km", ">15km"]:
    pct = 100 * last[b] / wb_only
    print(f"  {b:15} {int(last[b]):>9,} ({pct:5.1f}%)")
print(f"  TOTAL WB ONLY:  {int(wb_only):>9,}")
near = last["0-2.5km"] + last["2.5-5km"]
near_pct = 100 * near / wb_only
print(f"  Within 5 km:    {int(near):>9,} ({near_pct:.1f}%) — 'consensus' bloc territory")
deep = last[">15km"]
deep_pct = 100 * deep / wb_only
print(f"  Deeper than 15 km: {int(deep):>9,} ({deep_pct:.1f}%) — would require evacuation")

# --- ana_08: Growth rates by distance bucket ---
print("\n=== ana_08 ===")
first = ej_wb.iloc[0]

raw_evidence.label: What the Green Line is and why distance from it matters
raw_evidence.content: The Green Line is the 1949 armistice line that separated Israel from Jordanian-controlled West Bank and Egyptian-controlled Gaza until the 1967 Six-Day War. Its name comes literally from the green grease pencil used on the armistice map. Since 1967 it has functioned as the de-facto reference border in every serious peace plan: settlements close to the line are inside what negotiators call 'consensus blocs' (Gush Etzion, Ma'ale Adumim, Modi'in Illit, Ariel) that Israel would expect to keep through a land swap; settlements deep beyond it are the ones any two-state agreement would require evacuating. So the 0-2.5 km, 2.5-5 km, 5-15 km, and >15 km buckets in the dataset are not just geometric — each one corresponds to a different political category. Around 75-85% of West Bank settlers live close to the Green Line in major blocs adjacent to Israeli urban areas; the residual that live deep inside the West Bank are the politically hardest to relocate.

raw_evidence.label: Settlement blocs vs deep settlements — the political geography
raw_evidence.content: Inside the West Bank, distance from the Green Line is a proxy for political category. Settlements within a few kilometres of the line — Modi'in Illit, Ma'ale Adumim, the Gush Etzion bloc — are 'consensus' settlements that nearly every Israeli peace plan since Olmert assumes Israel will keep through a one-for-one land swap. Settlements deep in the West Bank (>15 km) are the ones any serious agreement would require evacuating; a Peace Now-aligned analysis estimated about 150,000 settlers would need to be evacuated and resettled. So the 'distance from green line' columns in population.ej.wb.csv are effectively a political map: 0-2.5 km is the part Israel expects to keep, >15 km is the part it would need to dismantle. Watching how each of those buckets has grown since 1998 is therefore a political story disguised as a geometry one.

raw_evidence.label: Settler population by distance from the Green Line, 2021
raw_evidence.content: In 2021, of the 739,682 Jews living beyond the 1967 Green Line, 31.5% were in East Jerusalem, 24.3% within 2.5 km of the line, 18.8% in the 2.5-5 km band, 15.2% between 5 and 15 km, and 10.2% deeper than 15 km. Looking at the West Bank only (506,558 settlers, excluding East Jerusalem), 62.8% live within 5 km of the Green Line — the 'consensus bloc' territory most peace plans assume Israel would keep through a land swap (det_06) — while 14.9% live deeper than 15 km, exactly the population that any two-state agreement would require evacuating.

total_2021 = sum(last[b] for b in buckets)
print(f"\n2021 totals across all buckets: {int(total_2021):,}")
print("2021 share by bucket:")
for b in buckets:
    pct = 100 * last[b] / total_2021
    print(f"  {b:15} {int(last[b]):>9,} ({pct:5.1f}%)")

# Compute share within West Bank only (excluding East Jerusalem)

wb_only = sum(last[b] for b in buckets if b != "East.Jerusalem")
for b in ["0-2.5km", "2.5-5km", "5-15km", ">15km"]:

    print(f"  {b:15} {int(last[b]):>9,} ({pct:5.1f}%)")
print(f"  TOTAL WB ONLY:  {int(wb_only):>9,}")
near = last["0-2.5km"] + last["2.5-5km"]
near_pct = 100 * near / wb_only
print(f"  Within 5 km:    {int(near):>9,} ({near_pct:.1f}%) — 'consensus' bloc territory")

Its name comes literally from the green grease pencil used on the armistice map. Since 1967 it has functioned as the de-facto reference border in every serious peace plan: settlements close to the line are inside what negotiators call 'consensus blocs' (Gush Etzion, Ma'ale Adumim, Modi'in Illit, Ariel) that Israel would expect to keep through a land swap; settlements deep beyond it are the ones any two-state agreement would require evacuating. Around 75-85% of West Bank settlers live close to the Green Line in major blocs adjacent to Israeli urban areas; the residual that live deep inside the West Bank are the politically hardest to relocate.

raw_evidence.label: What the Green Line is and why distance from it matters
raw_evidence.content: The Green Line is the 1949 armistice line that separated Israel from Jordanian-controlled West Bank and Egyptian-controlled Gaza until the 1967 Six-Day War. Its name comes literally from the green grease pencil used on the armistice map. Since 1967 it has functioned as the de-facto reference border in every serious peace plan: settlements close to the line are inside what negotiators call 'consensus blocs' (Gush Etzion, Ma'ale Adumim, Modi'in Illit, Ariel) that Israel would expect to keep through a land swap; settlements deep beyond it are the ones any two-state agreement would require evacuating. So the 0-2.5 km, 2.5-5 km, 5-15 km, and >15 km buckets in the dataset are not just geometric — each one corresponds to a different political category. Around 75-85% of West Bank settlers live close to the Green Line in major blocs adjacent to Israeli urban areas; the residual that live deep inside the West Bank are the politically hardest to relocate.

Settlements within a few kilometres of the line — Modi'in Illit, Ma'ale Adumim, the Gush Etzion bloc — are 'consensus' settlements that nearly every Israeli peace plan since Olmert assumes Israel will keep through a one-for-one land swap. raw_evidence.label: What the Green Line is and why distance from it matters
raw_evidence.content: The Green Line is the 1949 armistice line that separated Israel from Jordanian-controlled West Bank and Egyptian-controlled Gaza until the 1967 Six-Day War. Its name comes literally from the green grease pencil used on the armistice map. Since 1967 it has functioned as the de-facto reference border in every serious peace plan: settlements close to the line are inside what negotiators call 'consensus blocs' (Gush Etzion, Ma'ale Adumim, Modi'in Illit, Ariel) that Israel would expect to keep through a land swap; settlements deep beyond it are the ones any two-state agreement would require evacuating. So the 0-2.5 km, 2.5-5 km, 5-15 km, and >15 km buckets in the dataset are not just geometric — each one corresponds to a different political category. Around 75-85% of West Bank settlers live close to the Green Line in major blocs adjacent to Israeli urban areas; the residual that live deep inside the West Bank are the politically hardest to relocate.

raw_evidence.label: Settler population by distance from the Green Line, 2021
raw_evidence.content: In 2021, of the 739,682 Jews living beyond the 1967 Green Line, 31.5% were in East Jerusalem, 24.3% within 2.5 km of the line, 18.8% in the 2.5-5 km band, 15.2% between 5 and 15 km, and 10.2% deeper than 15 km. Looking at the West Bank only (506,558 settlers, excluding East Jerusalem), 62.8% live within 5 km of the Green Line — the 'consensus bloc' territory most peace plans assume Israel would keep through a land swap (det_06) — while 14.9% live deeper than 15 km, exactly the population that any two-state agreement would require evacuating.

raw_evidence.content: The Green Line is the 1949 armistice line that separated Israel from Jordanian-controlled West Bank and Egyptian-controlled Gaza until the 1967 Six-Day War. Its name comes literally from the green grease pencil used on the armistice map. Since 1967 it has functioned as the de-facto reference border in every serious peace plan: settlements close to the line are inside what negotiators call 'consensus blocs' (Gush Etzion, Ma'ale Adumim, Modi'in Illit, Ariel) that Israel would expect to keep through a land swap; settlements deep beyond it are the ones any two-state agreement would require evacuating. Around 75-85% of West Bank settlers live close to the Green Line in major blocs adjacent to Israeli urban areas; the residual that live deep inside the West Bank are the politically hardest to relocate.

Its name comes literally from the green grease pencil used on the armistice map. Since 1967 it has functioned as the de-facto reference border in every serious peace plan: settlements close to the line are inside what negotiators call 'consensus blocs' (Gush Etzion, Ma'ale Adumim, Modi'in Illit, Ariel) that Israel would expect to keep through a land swap; settlements deep beyond it are the ones any two-state agreement would require evacuating. Around 75-85% of West Bank settlers live close to the Green Line in major blocs adjacent to Israeli urban areas; the residual that live deep inside the West Bank are the politically hardest to relocate.

raw_evidence.label: What the Green Line is and why distance from it matters
raw_evidence.content: The Green Line is the 1949 armistice line that separated Israel from Jordanian-controlled West Bank and Egyptian-controlled Gaza until the 1967 Six-Day War. Its name comes literally from the green grease pencil used on the armistice map. Since 1967 it has functioned as the de-facto reference border in every serious peace plan: settlements close to the line are inside what negotiators call 'consensus blocs' (Gush Etzion, Ma'ale Adumim, Modi'in Illit, Ariel) that Israel would expect to keep through a land swap; settlements deep beyond it are the ones any two-state agreement would require evacuating. So the 0-2.5 km, 2.5-5 km, 5-15 km, and >15 km buckets in the dataset are not just geometric — each one corresponds to a different political category. Around 75-85% of West Bank settlers live close to the Green Line in major blocs adjacent to Israeli urban areas; the residual that live deep inside the West Bank are the politically hardest to relocate.

Settlements within a few kilometres of the line — Modi'in Illit, Ma'ale Adumim, the Gush Etzion bloc — are 'consensus' settlements that nearly every Israeli peace plan since Olmert assumes Israel will keep through a one-for-one land swap. Source: Israeli annexation of East Jerusalem — Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli_annexation_of_East_Jerusalem) Facts: Israel passed the Jerusalem Law in 1980, declaring a unified Jerusalem the capital and effectively annexing East Jerusalem; UN Security Council Resolution 478 declared the law null and void Source: East Jerusalem — B'Tselem (https://www.btselem.org/jerusalem) Facts: In 1967 only a few hundred Jews lived in East Jerusalem after the 1948 expulsions; The annexed area is currently home to at least 350,000 Palestinians and around 209,000 Israeli settlers

raw_evidence.label: Why East Jerusalem sits in its own column
raw_evidence.content: East Jerusalem is treated separately from the West Bank in this dataset for a reason. Israel formally annexed East Jerusalem in 1980 through the Jerusalem Law and applies Israeli civilian law there; the United Nations Security Council declared the annexation 'null and void' in Resolution 478 and most countries do not recognise it. The result is a population that Israel counts as 'Israeli' but most of the world counts as occupied: in 1967 only a few hundred Jews lived in East Jerusalem; by mid-1993 about 155,000 Jews and 150,000 Palestinians; by recent reporting roughly 209,000 Israeli settlers and 350,000 Palestinians. So when the CSV shows the East Jerusalem Jewish column climbing from ~158,000 in 1998 to ~233,000 in 2021, every one of those people is in territory that international law treats as occupied — which is why The Economist counts them as settlers even though Israel does not.

Source: Israel's growing settlements force stark choices about its future (The Economist, 2019-02-02) (https://www.economist.com/graphic-detail/2019/02/02/israels-growing-settlements-) Facts: 'The country cannot remain Jewish and democratic while controlling the entire Holy Land'; 'Between the Mediterranean and the Jordan river, the overall number of Arabs has caught up with that of Jews, and may soon exceed them.' | det_08: Caveats the analyst should preserve. Source: Israel's growing settlements force stark choices about its future (The Economist, 2019-02-02) (https://www.economist.com/graphic-detail/2019/02/02/israels-growing-settlements-) Facts: Post-2018 figures in the dataset are projections, not census counts

raw_evidence.label: The demographic 'trilemma' framing
raw_evidence.content: The Economist's 2019 framing rests on a trilemma the data is meant to dramatise: Israel is committed to being (a) Jewish-majority, (b) democratic, and (c) in control of the entire territory between the Jordan river and the Mediterranean. These three goals are mutually compatible only as long as Jews outnumber Arabs in the combined territory; once the populations cross, Israel can pick at most two of the three. The combined CSVs let you watch that crossover happen: by adding Israel + East Jerusalem + West Bank Jews on one side, and Israel + East Jerusalem + West Bank + Gaza Arabs on the other, the projected lines meet around 2018-2021. The piece is not arguing for any particular resolution — it is showing why expanding settlements squeezes the trilemma harder over time.

raw_evidence.label: Caveats the analyst should preserve
raw_evidence.content: Three caveats need to live in the prose, not in a footnote. First, post-2018 numbers in every column are projections, not census counts; the Jewish settler trajectory is built from Peace Now's reading of construction plans and tenders, the Israeli/Palestinian totals are from official statistical projections. Second, the 'Arab' and 'Jewish' columns are religious/national categorisations carried over from each statistical agency — they aren't fine-grained ethnicity buckets, and East Jerusalem Palestinians who hold Israeli residency permits are not Israeli citizens. Third, Gaza data ends in 2021 and predates the post-2023 destruction — readers familiar with later events should not assume the 2021 line projects forward as a population curve.

raw_evidence.label: The demographic 'trilemma' framing
raw_evidence.content: The Economist's 2019 framing rests on a trilemma the data is meant to dramatise: Israel is committed to being (a) Jewish-majority, (b) democratic, and (c) in control of the entire territory between the Jordan river and the Mediterranean. These three goals are mutually compatible only as long as Jews outnumber Arabs in the combined territory; once the populations cross, Israel can pick at most two of the three. The combined CSVs let you watch that crossover happen: by adding Israel + East Jerusalem + West Bank Jews on one side, and Israel + East Jerusalem + West Bank + Gaza Arabs on the other, the projected lines meet around 2018-2021. The piece is not arguing for any particular resolution — it is showing why expanding settlements squeezes the trilemma harder over time.

raw_evidence.label: Caveats the analyst should preserve
raw_evidence.content: Three caveats need to live in the prose, not in a footnote. First, post-2018 numbers in every column are projections, not census counts; the Jewish settler trajectory is built from Peace Now's reading of construction plans and tenders, the Israeli/Palestinian totals are from official statistical projections. Second, the 'Arab' and 'Jewish' columns are religious/national categorisations carried over from each statistical agency — they aren't fine-grained ethnicity buckets, and East Jerusalem Palestinians who hold Israeli residency permits are not Israeli citizens. Third, Gaza data ends in 2021 and predates the post-2023 destruction — readers familiar with later events should not assume the 2021 line projects forward as a population curve.
